title: ENIAC was programmed by plugging cables, and its first programmers were six women

cover.alt: Tall black panels of the ENIAC computer covered in switches, dials and plugged cables, preserved at the University of Pennsylvania.

body: **ENIAC**, completed in 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania and unveiled to the press on 15 February 1946, was the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer. Designed by John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert to calculate artillery firing tables for the US Army, it held about 18,000 vacuum tubes, 7,200 crystal diodes, 70,000 resistors and around 5 million hand-soldered joints, weighed more than 27 tonnes and drew 150 kW. It had no stored program: to set up a problem, its six original programmers, Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas and Ruth Lichterman, wired plugboards and set switches on its function tables, work that could take days after weeks of planning. Once running, its 5,000 additions a second made it about a thousand times faster than the electromechanical machines of the day.

slides.alt: Two women standing at ENIAC's tall control panels, working with cables and switches.
slides.caption: Two of ENIAC's programmers at its control panels. Plugging cables and setting switches was the programming.

slides.question: About how many vacuum tubes did ENIAC contain?
slides.explanation: About 18,000 vacuum tubes, plus 7,200 crystal diodes, 6,000 relays, 70,000 resistors and 10,000 capacitors, in a machine roughly 30 m long and 3 m tall.

slides.heading: What went into ENIAC
slides.note: Joined by about 5 million hand-soldered connections

slides.text: We had a tube fail about every two days and we could locate the problem within 15 minutes.
slides.attribution: J. Presper Eckert, co-designer of ENIAC

slides.heading: A secret first job
slides.text: Before the public ever saw it, ENIAC spent December 1945 on a feasibility study for the thermonuclear weapon, the hydrogen bomb, for Los Alamos. It went on computing until 11:45 p.m. on 2 October 1955, when it was retired in favour of its successors EDVAC and ORDVAC.

slides.question: How was ENIAC told what to compute?
options: By plugging cables and setting switches
By typing commands at a keyboard
By reading a program from paper tape
By loading a program into its memory
slides.explanation: ENIAC had no stored program. Its programmers wired plugboards and set switches on portable function tables, so changing the problem could take days.
